stimulus.text: The trial of John Peter Zenger, as pictured in an image published between 1877 and 1896. A crowded courtroom: three wigged judges sit on a raised bench, a lawyer stands addressing them, and a jury box and royal arms are visible on the wall.
stimulus.source_note: Image published 1877–1896, picturing the Zenger trial of 1735; public domain (pre-1930). The image is a 19th-century imagining, not a 1735 record.

source: original; stimulus is a real historical image from the shared pool

books.section: E. The Development of Self-Government in Britain's New World Colonies

stem: In 1735, printer John Peter Zenger was acquitted of seditious libel after criticizing New York's royal governor. Which broader development best explains why this trial mattered?

options.text: That it established the legal right of colonists to own enslaved people as property.
options.misconception: The trial concerned libel and the press, not slavery; it established no right about enslaved property.

options.text: That it became a landmark for press freedom as colonists asserted English liberties.
That it ended the Navigation Acts.
options.misconception: The Navigation Acts remained in force long after 1735; the trial did not touch them.

options.text: That it caused the First Great Awakening by inspiring Whitefield's preaching tours.
options.misconception: The Great Awakening was a separate religious movement of the 1730s and 1740s; the trial did not cause it.

rationales.general:
1. See the scene. A printer on trial for criticizing the royal governor, a jury of ordinary New Yorkers deciding.
2. See the result. Acquittal — the jury refused to convict.
3. Ask why it mattered beyond one printer. Colonists were claiming the liberties of English subjects against royal power.
4. Keep the limit in mind. No law changed; truth stayed no defense on the books.
Remember: Zenger mattered as a landmark of English liberties claimed in America — a jury's no, not a new law.
rationales.B: Zenger's acquittal became a landmark for freedom of the press: a colonial printer, tried for criticizing the royal governor, was freed by a jury of his neighbors. It belongs to the broader context of colonists asserting English liberties — alongside the press culture Franklin built and the Enlightenment's ideas — against royal authority. Background: the trial changed no law; the judge had barred the truth defense and truth stayed no defense on the books. What it showed was a jury checking a governor.
rationales.A: The trial concerned libel and the press, not slavery; it established no right about enslaved property.
rationales.C: The Navigation Acts remained in force long after 1735; the trial did not touch them.
rationales.D: The Great Awakening was a separate religious movement of the 1730s and 1740s; the trial did not cause it.
